Here is a structured study guide for your Vite/React app, with all content extracted directly from the attached PDFs. Each module uses "Learn" facts for flip cards or interactive displays, plus multiple-choice quizzes (a-d options, with answers).

Endocrine System (file:6)
Learn Facts
Endocrine system releases hormones into bloodstream for body-wide effects, unlike nervous system's quick, local neurotransmitters.
​
Hypothalamus controls pituitary with 9 releasing/inhibiting hormones; pituitary is "master gland".
​
Pituitary anterior lobe hormones: FSH/LH (gonads), TSH (thyroid), ACTH (adrenal), PRL (milk), GH (growth).
​
Thyroid produces T3/T4 for metabolism; parathyroid PTH raises blood Ca2+; adrenal cortex glucocorticoids like cortisol for stress.
​
Pancreas: insulin lowers glucose, glucagon raises it; negative feedback regulates most hormone levels.
​

Quiz Questions
Which system uses only chemical messengers via blood, with slower but longer effects?
a) Nervous
b) Endocrine
c) Muscular
d) Lymphatic
(Answer: b)
​

Hypothalamus produces how many hormones to regulate anterior pituitary?
a) 2
b) 6
c) 9
d) 12
(Answer: c)
​

Which hormone from beta cells lowers blood glucose?
a) Glucagon
b) Cortisol
c) Insulin
d) GH
(Answer: c)
​

TSH from pituitary stimulates which gland?
a) Adrenal
b) Thyroid
c) Pancreas
d) Pineal
(Answer: b)
​

What opposes calcitonin to raise blood Ca2+?
a) Insulin
b) PTH
c) T3/T4
d) ADH
(Answer: b)
​

Heart Anatomy (files:4,5)
Learn Facts
Heart wall: epicardium (outer serous), myocardium (muscular pump), endocardium (inner lining).

Four chambers: atria receive blood (with auricles), ventricles pump (left thicker for systemic circulation).

Valves: AV (tricuspid right, mitral/bicuspid left with chordae tendineae), semilunar (pulmonary, aortic).

Conduction: SA node (pacemaker in right atrium), AV node, bundle branches, Purkinje fibers.
​
ECG: P wave (atrial depol), QRS (ventricular depol), T wave (ventricular repol).

Quiz Questions
Which heart layer is cardiac muscle for pumping?
a) Epicardium
b) Endocardium
c) Myocardium
d) Pericardium
(Answer: c)

Right AV valve with 3 cusps?
a) Mitral
b) Aortic
c) Tricuspid
d) Pulmonary
(Answer: c)
​

Pacemaker initiating heartbeat?
a) AV node
b) SA node
c) Purkinje fibers
d) Bundle branches
(Answer: b)
​

QRS complex shows?
a) Atrial repolarization
b) Ventricular depolarization
c) SA node firing
d) Ventricular relaxation
(Answer: b)
​

Septum between ventricles called?
a) Interatrial
b) Interventricular
c) Coronary sulcus
d) Fossa ovalis
(Answer: b)

Endocrine PDF – Module 1 (Slides 1–8-ish)
Learn Items (for “Learn” view + flip cards)
Nervous vs Endocrine Basics

Endocrine system: hormones released into the bloodstream, effects may take hours but last longer.
​

Nervous system: uses neurotransmitters, effects in milliseconds, brief duration.
​

Cell Communication Mechanisms

Gap junctions: pores allowing signaling chemicals to move cell to cell.
​

Neurotransmitters: released from neurons across synaptic gaps.
​

Paracrine (local) hormones: act on nearby cells in tissue fluid.
​

Hormones (strict): chemical messengers traveling in bloodstream to distant targets.
​

Differences: Nervous vs Endocrine

Means: nervous has electrical + chemical; endocrine only chemical.
​

Speed: nervous reacts 1–10 msec and stops quickly; endocrine reacts more slowly (seconds–days), effects can persist for weeks.
​

Adaptation: nervous adapts quickly and response declines; endocrine responses are more persistent.
​

Area: nervous is targeted/specific (one organ); endocrine is general/widespread (many organs).
​

System Interactions & Overlap

Some chemicals act as both hormones and neurotransmitters (e.g., norepinephrine, dopamine, TRH, ADH).
​

Neuroendocrine cells (neurons) secrete hormones like oxytocin and catecholamines.
​

Both systems can act on same target (norepinephrine and glucagon both cause glycogen breakdown in liver).
​

Systems regulate each other: neurons trigger hormone secretion, hormones can stimulate or inhibit neurons.
​

General Functions of Hormones

Help regulate: extracellular fluid, metabolism, biological clock, cardiac and smooth muscle contraction, glandular secretion, some immune functions.
​

Support growth and development and reproduction.
​

Exocrine vs Endocrine Glands

Exocrine: secrete products into ducts to body cavities/surfaces (sweat, oil, mucous, digestive glands) with extracellular effects.
​

Endocrine: secrete hormones into bloodstream with intracellular effects; includes pituitary, thyroid, parathyroid, adrenal, pineal.
​

Some organs are mixed (2nd function): hypothalamus, thymus, pancreas, ovaries, testes, kidneys, stomach, liver, small intestine, skin, heart, placenta.
​

Hormones, Target Cells, and Components

Hormone: chemical messenger secreted into bloodstream that stimulates response in another tissue or organ.
​

Target cells have specific receptors for a hormone.
​

Endocrine system includes classic glands and hormone-producing cells in organs like brain, heart, and small intestine.
​

Major Endocrine Organs

Hypothalamus, pituitary, pineal, thyroid, parathyroids, thymus, adrenal glands, pancreas, gonads (ovaries/testes).
​

Control of Hormone Secretion

Regulated by nervous signals, blood chemistry, or other hormones.
​

Negative feedback: most common; changes in blood levels are reversed (e.g., T3/T4–TSH–TRH loop).
​

Positive feedback: hormone-caused change triggers more hormone release (e.g., oxytocin and uterine contractions).
​

Disorders can arise from hyposecretion or hypersecretion.
​

Thyroid Negative Feedback Example

Low T3/T4 or low metabolic rate → TRH from hypothalamus → TSH from anterior pituitary → T3/T4 release from thyroid.
​

Elevated T3 inhibits TRH and TSH (classic negative feedback).
​

Positive Feedback – Oxytocin

Oxytocin stimulates uterine contractions; contractions stimulate more oxytocin release.
​

Suckling stimulates nerve endings → hypothalamus → posterior pituitary → oxytocin → milk ejection.
​

Hypothalamus–Pituitary Overview

Both called master endocrine glands because their hormones control other glands.
​

Hypothalamus is brain region above pituitary, receives input from cortex, thalamus, limbic system, and internal organs.
​

Hypothalamus controls pituitary with 9 releasing and inhibiting hormones.
​

Pituitary Anatomy (Basic)

Pea-sized gland in sella turcica, attached to brain via infundibulum.
​

Anterior lobe ≈ 75% (glandular), develops from roof of mouth.
​

Posterior lobe ≈ 25%, made of axon terminals from hypothalamic neurons and pituicytes.
​

Full Question Bank for Module 1 (MCQs)
You can tag these in code as type: "practice" vs type: "quiz".

The endocrine system primarily communicates using:
a) Electrical impulses
b) Neurotransmitters at synapses
c) Hormones in the bloodstream
d) Action potentials in neurons
Answer: c
​

Compared to the endocrine system, the nervous system response is:
a) Slower and longer lasting
b) Faster and longer lasting
c) Faster and shorter in duration
d) Slower and shorter in duration
Answer: c
​

Which communication method uses pores that directly connect neighboring cells?
a) Neurotransmitters
b) Hormones
c) Gap junctions
d) Paracrine signals
Answer: c
​

A local hormone that affects nearby cells in the same tissue is called a:
a) Neurotransmitter
b) Gap junction messenger
c) Paracrine hormone
d) Endocrine hormone
Answer: c
​

Which system uses both electrical and chemical signals?
a) Endocrine
b) Nervous
c) Lymphatic
d) Immune
Answer: b
​

Endocrine responses are typically:
a) Rapid and short-lived
b) Rapid and localized
c) Slow and localized
d) Slow and long-lasting
Answer: d
​

Which statement best describes endocrine effects?
a) Always limited to one organ
b) Targeted to a single synapse
c) Often general and widespread
d) Only in skeletal muscle

a) Calcitonin
b) Thyroxine
c) Norepinephrine
d) Insulin

a) Extracellular fluid

a) Growth and development
b) Reproduction

Exocrine glands release their products:
a) Directly into blood
b) Into ducts to body surfaces or cavities

d) Into the cerebrospinal fluid

Which is an example of an exocrine gland product?
a) Insulin
b) Thyroxine
c) Sweat
d) ADH
Answer: c
​

Endocrine glands are characterized by:
a) Ducts opening to body surfaces
b) Hormone secretion into the bloodstream
c) Only local effects
d) Storage of neurotransmitters
Answer: b
​

Which organ has a secondary endocrine function?
a) Sweat gland
b) Lung
c) Heart
d) Skeletal muscle
Answer: c

A hormone is best defined as:
a) Any neurotransmitter in the brain
b) Chemical messenger secreted into bloodstream affecting distant tissues
c) Any molecule secreted into intestines
d) A local paracrine factor only
Answer: b
​

Cells that have specific receptors for a hormone are called:
a) Neuroglia
b) Target cells
c) Exocrine cells
d) Erythrocytes
Answer: b
​

Which of these is NOT a major endocrine organ listed in the PDF?
a) Thyroid gland
b) Parathyroid glands
c) Adrenal glands
d) Appendix
Answer: d
​

What type of feedback is most common in hormone regulation?
a) Negative feedback
b) Positive feedback
c) Neutral feedback
d) Recursive feedback
Answer: a
​

In the T3/T4 feedback loop, which hormone directly stimulates thyroid follicular cells?
a) TRH
b) TSH
c) ACTH
d) GH
Answer: b
​

Elevated T3 levels will:
a) Stimulate more TRH and TSH release
b) Inhibit TRH and TSH release
c) Have no effect on TRH
d) Only increase ACTH
Answer: b
​

Oxytocin during labor is an example of:
a) Negative feedback
b) Positive feedback
c) Neutral feedback
d) Feedforward inhibition
Answer: b
​

Which event directly increases oxytocin release for milk ejection?
a) Rising blood glucose
b) Elevated TSH
c) Suckling infant stimulating nerve endings
d) Low blood pressure in aorta
Answer: c
​

The hypothalamus controls the pituitary gland using:
a) Only nerve impulses
b) Nine releasing and inhibiting hormones
c) Digestive enzymes
d) Gap junctions exclusively
Answer: b
​

The anterior pituitary develops from:
a) Neural tissue in the brainstem
b) Roof of the mouth
c) Spinal cord
d) Adrenal cortex
Answer: b
​

The posterior pituitary mainly consists of:
a) Glandular epithelial cells
b) Axon terminals of hypothalamic neurons and pituicytes
c) Skeletal muscle fibers
d) Chondrocytes
Answer: b

Here is Endocrine Module 2 (next ~6–8 “slides” from the same PDF): focused on hypothalamic–pituitary hormones, GH, posterior pituitary, pineal, thymus, and thyroid.
​

You can treat this as another chunk in your app: moduleId: endocrine-2.

Endocrine PDF – Module 2
(Hypothalamus–Pituitary–Pineal–Thymus–Thyroid)

Learn Items (for Learn view / flip cards)
Hypothalamo–Hypophyseal Portal System

Hypothalamus secretes releasing/inhibiting hormones into a portal system that goes directly to the anterior pituitary.
​

Key hypothalamic hormones: GnRH, TRH, CRH, PRH, PIH, GHRH, somatostatin.
​

Anterior Pituitary Tropic Hormones

Anterior pituitary (adenohypophysis) secretes FSH, LH, TSH, ACTH, PRL, GH under hypothalamic control.
​

Tropic hormones target other endocrine glands (gonads, thyroid, adrenal cortex, etc.).
​

GH and IGF Functions

GH from somatotropes promotes tissue growth directly (mitosis, differentiation) and indirectly via IGF‑I from liver.
​

GH–IGF increase protein synthesis, enhance amino acid transport, reduce protein breakdown.
​

They stimulate lipid metabolism (FFA and glycerol release), glucose‑sparing, and promote Na⁺, K⁺, Cl⁻ retention and Ca²⁺ absorption.
​

Regulation of hGH

Low blood glucose → GHRH from hypothalamus → more hGH → glycogen breakdown to glucose in liver.
​

High blood glucose → GHIH from hypothalamus → less hGH → less glycogen breakdown.
​

Diabetogenic Effect & Aging of GH

Excess GH raises blood glucose, causing continual insulin release and potential beta‑cell burnout, contributing to diabetes mellitus.
​

In childhood/adolescence GH drives bone, cartilage, muscle growth; in adults it increases osteoblastic activity and bone thickening.
​

GH levels are higher in deep sleep, after high‑protein meals, and vigorous exercise, and lower after high‑carb meals; levels fall to about ¼ by age 75.
​

TSH – Thyroid‑Stimulating Hormone

Hypothalamus regulates thyrotrophs, which produce TSH.
​

TSH stimulates thyroid to synthesize and secrete T3 and T4, raising metabolic rate.
​

FSH – Follicle‑Stimulating Hormone

GnRH from hypothalamus controls gonadotrophs which release FSH.
​

FSH forms ovarian follicles and stimulates estrogen secretion in females, and stimulates sperm production in testes in males.
​

LH – Luteinizing Hormone

GnRH stimulates gonadotrophs to release LH.
​

In females: stimulates estrogen secretion, ovulation, corpus luteum formation, and progesterone secretion.
​

In males: stimulates interstitial cells to secrete testosterone.
​

PRL – Prolactin

Hypothalamus controls lactotrophs; they produce prolactin.
​

Under proper conditions, PRL causes milk production; suckling reduces hypothalamic inhibition, raising PRL and milk production; when nursing stops, milk production slows.
​

ACTH and MSH

Hypothalamic releasing hormones stimulate corticotrophs to secrete ACTH and MSH.
​

ACTH stimulates adrenal cortex cells to produce glucocorticoids.
​

MSH function in humans is uncertain (known to increase skin pigmentation in frogs).
​

Posterior Pituitary – ADH and Oxytocin

Posterior pituitary (neurohypophysis) does not synthesize hormones; it stores and releases ADH and oxytocin from hypothalamic axon terminals.
​

Oxytocin: during delivery, cervical stretch → more uterine contractions; after delivery, suckling/hearing baby → milk ejection via myoepithelial contraction.
​

ADH (vasopressin): decreases urine production, decreases sweating, increases blood pressure.
​

Regulation of ADH

Dehydration → ADH release → kidneys retain water, sweat glands reduce water loss, arterioles constrict to raise BP.
​

Overhydration → ADH inhibition → more urine, less water retention.
​

Pineal Gland and Melatonin

Pineal gland: peak secretion at 1–5 years; about 75% lower by puberty.
​

Produces serotonin by day and converts it to melatonin at night; melatonin may regulate timing of puberty.
​

Melatonin is increased in Seasonal Affective Disorder (SAD) and PMS; phototherapy can reduce symptoms.
​

Light Regulation of Melatonin

In darkness, fewer impulses from retina → pathway through suprachiasmatic nucleus and superior cervical ganglion → lack of norepinephrine → increased melatonin → sleepiness.
​

In light, norepinephrine inhibits melatonin secretion → less sleepiness.
​

Thymus

Located in mediastinum superior to heart; undergoes involution after puberty.
​

Secretes thymopoietin and thymosins, which regulate development and later activation of T‑lymphocytes.
​

Thyroid Gland & Hormones

Largest endocrine gland with high blood flow; two lobes with isthmus on anterior/lateral trachea.
​

Follicular cells in follicles secrete T3 and T4, which increase metabolic rate and O₂ consumption, heat production, heart rate/contractility, respiratory rate, appetite, and breakdown of carbs, lipids, and proteins.
​

C (parafollicular) cells secrete calcitonin, decreasing blood Ca²⁺ by promoting bone deposition, especially in children.
​

Here is Endocrine Module 3: final 6–8 “pages” worth, focused on stress, aging, and disorders (thyroid, parathyroid, adrenal, pancreas/diabetes, hyperinsulinism). This closes out the endocrine PDF content for your app.
​

Endocrine PDF – Module 3
(Stress, Aging, Endocrine Disorders & Diabetes)

Learn Items (for Learn/flip cards)
Stress, Immune System, and Disease

Stress can contribute to disease by inhibiting the immune system, increasing risk of hypertension, asthma, migraine, gastritis, colitis, and depression.
​

Macrophages secrete interleukin‑1, linking stress and immunity by stimulating immune substance production; these immune substances then suppress interleukin‑1 in a feedback loop.
​

Endocrine Changes with Aging

Human growth hormone production decreases with age, leading to muscle atrophy.
​

TSH production increases with age to stimulate the thyroid, but metabolic rate still decreases, body fat increases, and hypothyroidism becomes more common.
​

Thymus is replaced with adipose tissue after puberty; adrenal glands produce less cortisol and aldosterone.
​

Receptor sensitivity to glucose declines; ovaries stop responding to gonadotropins, reducing estrogen and contributing to osteoporosis and atherosclerosis.
​

General Endocrine Disorders

Variations in hormone concentration and target‑cell sensitivity cause noticeable body effects.
​

Hyposecretion: inadequate hormone release, often from tumors/lesions destroying glands; example: head trauma damaging pituitary → ADH deficiency → diabetes insipidus with chronic polyuria.
​

Hypersecretion: excessive hormone release from tumors or autoimmune disorders; example: toxic goiter (Graves disease) where antibodies mimic TSH on the thyroid.
​

Pituitary Disorders – GH Imbalance

Hypersecretion of GH: acromegaly in adults (thickening of bones and soft tissues).
​

Childhood/adolescence: GH oversecretion causes gigantism; GH hyposecretion causes dwarfism.
​

Thyroid Disorders – Hyper and Hypo

Hyperthyroidism: symptoms include weight loss, tremors, nervousness, and exophthalmos.
​

Endemic goiter: iodine deficiency → no thyroid hormone → no negative feedback → elevated TSH and enlarged thyroid.
​

Toxic goiter (Graves disease): antibodies mimic TSH, causing high thyroid hormone and exophthalmos.
​

Congenital hypothyroidism (low TH in infants): abnormal bone development, thick facial features, low temp, lethargy, brain damage, dwarfism/cretinism.
​

Myxedema (adult hypothyroidism): low metabolic rate, sluggishness, sleepiness, weight gain, constipation, dry skin/hair, cold sensitivity, increased blood pressure and tissue swelling.
​

Parathyroid Disorders

Hypoparathyroidism: often after surgical removal during thyroid surgery, can cause fatal tetany within 3–4 days.
​

Hyperparathyroidism: excess PTH from tumor → soft, fragile, deformed bones, increased blood Ca²⁺, and renal calculi (kidney stones).
​

Adrenal Disorders – Cortex

Cushing syndrome: excess cortical secretion → hyperglycemia, hypertension, weakness, edema, muscle and bone loss from protein catabolism, poor wound healing.
​

Cushing body changes: “buffalo hump” fat between shoulders and “moon face” with thin, spindly legs.
​

Adrenogenital syndrome (AGS): adrenal androgen hypersecretion often accompanying Cushing → external genital enlargement in children and early puberty, and masculinization in women (deeper voice, beard).
​

Addison’s disease: hyposecretion of glucocorticoids → hypoglycemia, muscle weakness, low BP, dehydration from low Na⁺, skin darkening similar to MSH effects, and risk of cardiac arrest.
​

Diabetes Mellitus – Core Features

Due to hyposecretion of insulin: signs include polyuria, polydipsia, polyphagia, plus hyperglycemia, glycosuria, and ketonuria.
​

Osmotic diuresis: blood glucose above renal transport maximum → glucose remains in urine, increases osmolarity, pulls water into urine.
​

Kidney tubules cannot reabsorb glucose fast enough without insulin, causing continued glucose and ketone loss and diuresis.
​

Types of Diabetes Mellitus

Type I (IDDM): ≈10% of cases; often autoimmune destruction of beta cells; usually diagnosed around age 12.
​

Type I treatment: diet, exercise, blood glucose monitoring, and insulin injections or pump.
​

Type II (NIDDM): ≈90%; insulin resistance with target cells failing to respond to insulin.
​

Type II risk factors: heredity, age over 40, and obesity; treatment is weight loss (diet + exercise) and oral meds that improve insulin secretion or sensitivity.
​

Pathology of Diabetes – Acute and Chronic

Acute: cells cannot absorb glucose, rely on fats and proteins → weight loss and weakness.
​

Increased fat catabolism → elevated FFA and ketone bodies; ketonuria causes osmotic diuresis with loss of Na⁺ and K⁺.
​

Ketoacidosis: ketones lowering blood pH → dyspnea and possibly diabetic coma if untreated.
​

Chronic hyperglycemia → neuropathy and cardiovascular damage due to atherosclerosis, affecting retina and kidneys (type I), causing heart failure and gangrene (type II).
​

Hyperinsulinism

Causes: excessive insulin injection or pancreatic islet tumor.
​

Leads to hypoglycemia, weakness, hunger, and triggers epinephrine, GH, and glucagon release with anxiety, sweating, and increased heart rate.
​

Insulin shock: uncorrected hyperinsulinism resulting in disorientation, convulsions, or unconsciousness.
​

Heart PDF – Module 1
(Basic Anatomy, Chambers, Valves, Layers)

Learn Items
Heart Position & Orientation

The heart lies in the mediastinum between the lungs, with a base (broad superior portion) and an apex that tilts left and rests just above the diaphragm.
​

It has anterior and inferior surfaces and right and left borders.
​

Pericardium and Heart Wall

Fibrous pericardium: tough dense irregular CT that protects, anchors, and prevents overstretching.
​

Serous pericardium: parietal and visceral (epicardium) layers with pericardial cavity and fluid between them.
​

Heart wall layers: epicardium (outer serous membrane), myocardium (thick cardiac muscle with fibrous skeleton), and endocardium (smooth inner lining continuous with vessel endothelium).

Chambers of the Heart

Four chambers: two superior atria (receiving chambers) and two inferior ventricles (pumping chambers).

Each atrium has an auricle that slightly increases volume and contains pectinate muscles; atrial walls are thin due to light workload.
​

Ventricles are separated by the interventricular septum and have internal ridges called trabeculae carneae.

Right Atrium and Right Ventricle

Right atrium receives blood from superior vena cava, inferior vena cava, and coronary sinus; interatrial septum contains fossa ovalis (remnant of foramen ovale).

Tricuspid (right AV) valve with three cusps leads to right ventricle.

Right ventricle forms most of the anterior surface; contains papillary muscles, trabeculae carneae, chordae tendineae, and opens into pulmonary trunk via pulmonary semilunar valve.
​

Left Atrium and Left Ventricle

Left atrium forms most of the base and receives four pulmonary veins (two right, two left).
​

Blood flows through bicuspid/mitral (left AV) valve with two cusps into the left ventricle.

Left ventricle forms the apex, has thickest myocardium, contains chordae tendineae and trabeculae carneae, and pumps through aortic semilunar valve into ascending aorta.
​

Openings to coronary arteries lie just above the aortic valve.
​

Myocardial Thickness and Function

Atria are thin‑walled and deliver blood to nearby ventricles.
​

Right ventricle pumps to low‑resistance lungs; left ventricle has the thickest wall to supply the systemic circulation.
​

Fibrous Skeleton and Valve Types

Fibrous skeleton: dense CT rings around valves, fused with interventricular septum; provides structural support, muscle attachment, and acts as an electrical insulator between atria and ventricles.
​

AV valves: right AV (tricuspid) and left AV (mitral/bicuspid) with chordae tendineae attaching cusps to papillary muscles.

Semilunar valves: pulmonary (right ventricle → pulmonary trunk) and aortic (left ventricle → aorta) control outflow from ventricles.

AV Valve Mechanics

When ventricles relax: pressure falls, semilunar valves close, AV valves open, and blood flows from atria into ventricles.
​

When ventricles contract: pressure rises, AV valves close; papillary muscles contract pulling on chordae tendineae to prevent prolapse; semilunar valves open and blood is ejected into great arteries.
​

Here’s Heart Module 2 (conduction, ECG, cardiac cycle, heart sounds, CO/HR), with mixed correct answer positions.

Heart PDF – Module 2
(Conduction System, ECG, Cardiac Cycle, CO & HR)

Learn Items
Cardiac Conduction System Basics

The heartbeat is myogenic and autorhythmic, originating within the heart with regular, spontaneous depolarization.
​

SA node in the right atrium acts as pacemaker, initiating each heartbeat and setting heart rate; fibrous skeleton insulates atria from ventricles.
​

Conduction Pathway

SA node → atrial myocardium → AV node (electrical gateway to ventricles).
​

AV bundle (bundle of His) carries signals from AV node into interventricular septum, where right and left bundle branches descend to the apex; Purkinje fibers spread upward through ventricular myocardium.
​

Firing Rates and Ectopic Pacemakers

SA node fires 90–100 times/min; AV node 40–50/min; ventricular fibers alone 20–40/min.
​

If both nodes are suppressed, ventricular rate is too low and an artificial pacemaker may be needed.
​

Extra beats from other sites are ectopic pacemakers; caffeine and nicotine increase their activity.
​

Timing of Atrial and Ventricular Excitation

SA node depolarization spreads through atria and to AV node in about 50 ms.
​

AV node delay (~100 ms) due to smaller fibers allows atria to finish contracting and filling the ventricles before ventricular contraction.
​

Excitation then spreads through both ventricles in about 50 ms.
​

Action Potential in Cardiac Muscle

Resting potential is about −90 mV; depolarization occurs as fast Na⁺ channels open and membrane potential peaks around +30 mV.
​

Plateau (200–250 ms) due to slow Ca²⁺ entry and SR release maintains contraction.
​

Repolarization occurs as Ca²⁺ channels close and K⁺ channels open; long refractory period prevents tetanus and allows filling.
​

Electrocardiogram (ECG) Components

ECG is a composite of all nodal and myocardial action potentials recorded on body surface.

P wave: SA node fires and atria depolarize, followed by atrial systole.

PQ interval: conduction time from atria to ventricles.
​

QRS complex: AV node fires, ventricles depolarize and contract (ventricular systole); atrial repolarization is masked.

T wave: ventricular repolarization just before diastole.

ECG Uses and Abnormalities

ECG helps diagnose conduction abnormalities, myocardial infarction, heart enlargement, and electrolyte or hormone imbalances.
​

Examples: no P waves, extrasystoles with abnormal QRS/T, or arrhythmias from AV node conduction failure (no effective pumping).
​

Cardiac Cycle Phases and Volumes

At 75 bpm, one cycle lasts 0.8 s: atrial systole 0.1 s, ventricular systole 0.3 s, quiescent period 0.4 s.
​

EDV: ~130 ml at end of diastole; ESV: ~60 ml at end of systole; stroke volume (SV) ≈ 70 ml = EDV − ESV.
​

Heart Sounds

S1 (“lubb”): louder, longer sound from closure of AV valves at start of ventricular systole.
​

S2 (“dupp”): softer, sharper sound from closure of semilunar valves at start of ventricular diastole.
​

S3 may occur during rapid ventricular filling, rarely heard in people over 30.
​

Cardiac Output and Heart Rate

Cardiac output (CO) = heart rate (HR) × stroke volume (SV); resting ~5.25 L/min (75 × 70 ml), typically 4–6 L/min.
​

CO can reach ~21 L/min in fit individuals and up to 35 L/min in elite athletes; cardiac reserve = max CO/rest CO.
​

Tachycardia: persistent resting HR > 100; bradycardia: HR < 60, common in endurance athletes (higher SV).
​

​Heart PDF – Module 3
(Autonomic HR Control, Stroke Volume, CHF, Risk Factors)

Learn Items
Cardiac Output and Reserve

Cardiac output (CO) is the amount ejected by each ventricle per minute: CO = HR × SV.
​

Resting CO ≈ 5.25 L/min (75 bpm × 70 ml), usually 4–6 L/min; during vigorous exercise CO can reach ~21 L/min in fit people and up to ~35 L/min in world‑class athletes.
​

Cardiac reserve = maximum CO ÷ CO at rest; it increases with fitness and decreases with disease (about 4–5 normally, 7–8 in athletes).
​

Heart Rate Basics

HR is measured from pulse; infants ~120 bpm, young adult females 72–80 bpm, young adult males 64–72 bpm; HR rises again in elderly.
​

Tachycardia: persistent resting HR > 100 bpm (due to stress, anxiety, drugs, heart disease, or increased body temperature).
​

Bradycardia: persistent resting HR < 60 bpm, common during sleep and in endurance‑trained athletes (who have higher stroke volume).
​

Chronotropic Effects and Cardiac Centers

Positive chronotropic agents increase HR; negative chronotropic agents decrease HR.
​

The cardiac center in the medulla oblongata has two neuronal pools: a cardioacceleratory center (sympathetic) and a cardioinhibitory center (parasympathetic).
​

Sympathetic Stimulation

Cardioacceleratory center stimulates sympathetic cardiac accelerator nerves to SA node, AV node, and myocardium.
​

These nerves release norepinephrine, which binds to β‑adrenergic receptors and increases HR (positive chronotropic effect).
​

CO peaks at HR of 160–180 bpm; sympathetic stimulation can push HR up to ~230 bpm, but very high rates reduce SV and CO due to less filling time.
​

Parasympathetic Stimulation

Cardioinhibitory center sends parasympathetic fibers via the vagus nerves: right vagus mainly to SA node, left vagus to AV node.
​

They release acetylcholine, opening K⁺ channels in nodal cells, hyperpolarizing them and slowing their firing rate, thus lowering HR.
​

Vagal tone maintains resting HR around 70–80 bpm; if vagus nerves are cut, SA node fires at its intrinsic rate (~100 bpm).
​

Inputs to the Cardiac Center

Higher brain centers (cortex, limbic system, hypothalamus) influence HR in response to sensory and emotional stimuli (e.g., fear, excitement).
​

Proprioceptors in muscles/joints signal activity changes, causing HR to rise at the start of exercise before metabolic demands change.
​

Baroreceptors in aorta and carotid arteries send pressure information: if BP falls, firing rate drops and cardiac center raises HR; if BP rises, firing rate increases and cardiac center lowers HR.
​

Chemoreceptors in aortic arch, carotid arteries, and medulla monitor pH, CO₂, and O₂; hypercapnia and acidosis stimulate the cardiac center to increase HR.
​

Chemical Influences on HR

Neurotransmitters (norepinephrine and epinephrine) using cAMP as a second messenger are potent cardiac stimulants.
​

Drugs: caffeine prolongs cAMP effects by inhibiting its breakdown; nicotine stimulates catecholamine secretion.
​

Thyroid hormone increases adrenergic receptors in the heart, raising sensitivity to sympathetic stimulation and HR.
​

Potassium has strong chronotropic effects: moderate K⁺ elevation makes myocardium less excitable and slows HR; very high K⁺ or very low K⁺ can severely disturb rhythm.
​

Stroke Volume Determinants

Stroke volume is governed by three main factors: preload, contractility, and afterload.
​

Preload: amount of tension in ventricular myocardium before contraction; increased preload increases SV (Frank–Starling law: SV ∝ EDV).
​

Contractility: force of contraction at a given preload; positive inotropic agents (e.g., norepinephrine, hypercalcemia, catecholamines, glucagon, digitalis) increase contractility; negative inotropic agents (e.g., hyperkalemia, hypocalcemia, hypoxia, hypercapnia) decrease it.
​

Afterload: pressure opposing semilunar valve opening (pressure in arteries); increased afterload decreases SV.
​

Effects of Exercise on CO

At the start of exercise, proprioceptors increase HR; ongoing muscular activity raises venous return, increasing preload and SV, so both HR and SV rise to increase CO.
​

Sustained exercise can cause ventricular hypertrophy; a larger SV allows a lower resting HR (e.g., 40–60 bpm) and increases cardiac reserve.
​

Congestive Heart Failure (CHF)

CHF: either ventricle fails to eject blood effectively, often due to coronary artery disease, hypertension, myocardial infarction, valve disorders, or congenital defects.
​

Left‑sided failure: blood backs up into lungs → pulmonary edema, suffocation, and tissue hypoxia.
​

Right‑sided failure: blood backs up in systemic circulation → peripheral edema and fluid accumulation in tissues.
​

Risk Factors for Heart Disease

Major risk factors: high blood cholesterol, high BP, cigarette smoking, obesity, and lack of regular exercise.
​

Other factors: diabetes mellitus, genetic predisposition, male gender, high fibrinogen levels, and left ventricular hypertrophy.
​

Blood PDF – Module 1
(Overview, Functions, Properties, Plasma, Formed Elements, Hematocrit, Hemopoiesis)

Learn Items
Body Fluids and Hematology

Cells are serviced by blood (plasma + cells) and interstitial fluid, which bathes body cells.
​

Nutrients and oxygen diffuse from blood → interstitial fluid → cells; wastes move in the reverse direction.
​

Hematology is the study of blood and blood disorders.
​

Functions of Blood

Transportation: carries O₂, CO₂, metabolic wastes, nutrients, heat, and hormones.
​

Regulation: helps regulate pH via buffers, body temperature via water’s coolant properties and vasodilation of surface vessels, and water content of cells via dissolved ions and proteins.
​

Protection: defends against disease and prevents blood loss (hemostasis).
​

Basic Properties of Blood

Adults have about 4–6 liters of blood composed of plasma (clear extracellular fluid) and formed elements (cells and platelets).
​

Blood is more viscous than water and flows more slowly, has a temperature of ~100.4°F, pH about 7.4 (7.35–7.45), and accounts for ~8% of body weight.
​

Blood Volume and Osmolarity

Average blood volume: males 5–6 L, females 4–5 L.
​

Negative feedback maintains blood volume and osmotic pressure.
​

If blood osmolarity is too high, fluid moves into blood and can cause high BP; if too low, fluid stays in tissues causing edema, sometimes from low plasma protein (diet or disease).
​

Blood Sampling Techniques

Venipuncture: sample from a vein (e.g., median cubital) with a syringe; veins are preferred over arteries because they have lower pressure and are closer to the surface.
​

Finger or heel stick: used by diabetics for daily blood sugar and commonly in infants.
​

Components and Hematocrit

Blood is ~55% plasma and ~45% cells; of the cells, ~99% are RBCs and <1% are WBCs and platelets.
​

Hematocrit is the percentage of blood volume occupied by cells.
​

Normal hematocrit: females 38–46% (avg 42%), males 40–54% (avg 46%), with higher male values influenced by testosterone.
​

Plasma and Plasma Proteins

Plasma: ~>90% water, ~7% proteins, and ~2% other solutes (enzymes, nutrients, wastes, hormones, electrolytes, gases).
​

If blood clots, the remaining fluid is serum.
​

Major plasma proteins:

Albumins: most abundant; contribute to viscosity and osmolarity, influencing blood pressure, flow, and fluid balance.
​

Globulins (alpha, beta, gamma): antibodies providing immune defense.
​

Fibrinogen: precursor of fibrin threads that form blood clots.
​

Liver makes most plasma proteins; globulins are produced by plasma cells from B lymphocytes.
​

Non‑protein Plasma Components

Nitrogenous compounds: amino acids and wastes (urea) from protein catabolism, normally removed by kidneys.
​

Nutrients include glucose, vitamins, fats, and minerals; some O₂ and CO₂ are carried in plasma.
​

Electrolytes, especially sodium (about 90% of plasma cations), contribute heavily to blood osmolarity.
​

Formed Elements Overview

Red blood cells (erythrocytes).
​

White blood cells (leukocytes):

Granular: neutrophils, eosinophils, basophils.
​

Agranular: lymphocytes (T cells, B cells, NK cells) and monocytes.
​

Platelets are special cell fragments important for clotting.
​

Hematocrit Disorders: Anemia and Polycythemia

Anemia: too few RBCs or too little hemoglobin.
​

Polycythemia: too many RBCs (>65%), which can result from dehydration, tissue hypoxia, or blood doping.
​

Blood Doping

Involves reinfusing stored RBCs before an athletic event to increase O₂ delivery.
​

Dangerous because it increases blood viscosity and forces the heart to work harder; banned by the Olympic committee.
​

Hemopoiesis – Sites and Stem Cells

Most blood cells have short lifespans and need continual replacement.
​

Embryonic yolk sac produces stem cells that colonize fetal bone marrow, liver, spleen, and thymus; liver stops producing blood cells at birth, but spleen and thymus remain involved with WBC production.
​

Lymphoid hemopoiesis occurs in lymphoid tissues (thymus, tonsils, lymph nodes, spleen, Peyer’s patches).
​

Red bone marrow produces RBCs, WBCs, and platelets from hemocytoblasts (pluripotent stem cells) that can differentiate into multiple lines; committed cells follow one specific lineage.
​

In adults, active red marrow is in flat bones (sternum, ribs, skull, pelvis) and heads of femur and humerus.
​

Production is stimulated by erythropoietin, thrombopoietin, and colony‑stimulating factors (CSFs).
​

Hemopoietic Growth Factors

Erythropoietin (EPO): from kidneys, increases RBC precursors.
​

Thrombopoietin (TPO): from liver, stimulates platelet formation.
​

Cytokines (CSFs and interleukins): local hormones in bone marrow stimulating WBC production.
​

Recombinant forms of these factors are used clinically (e.g., EPO for kidney disease anemia, CSFs for cancer chemo, TPO for platelet support).
​

​Blood PDF – Module 2
(RBC Structure, Hemoglobin, Erythropoiesis, Anemia, Sickle‑Cell)

Learn Items
RBC Structure and Function

New RBCs enter circulation at about 2 million per second.
​

Erythrocytes are biconcave discs (~7.5 μm wide, 2 μm thick at rim) with no organelles, maximizing surface area/volume for gas exchange.
​

Main function is gas transport: about 33% of cytoplasm is hemoglobin, carrying O₂ to tissues and CO₂ back to lungs.
​

RBCs contain carbonic anhydrase, which forms carbonic acid from CO₂ and water, important in gas transport and pH balance.
​

Erythropoiesis – Steps

Erythropoiesis produces ~2.5 million RBCs/second from hemocytoblasts in bone marrow.
​

First committed cell is the proerythroblast, which has receptors for EPO.
​

Erythroblasts multiply and synthesize hemoglobin, then become normoblasts that discard their nucleus to form reticulocytes.
​

Reticulocytes (with a network of ER) enter blood as 0.5–1.5% of RBCs; full development takes 3–5 days with cell size reduction, increased cell number, Hb synthesis, and nucleus loss; blood loss speeds this up.
​

Reticulocyte Count and Bone Marrow Status

Normal reticulocyte count: 0.5–1.5% of circulating RBCs.
​

Low reticulocyte count in anemia suggests bone marrow problems (e.g., leukemia, nutritional deficit, or lack of EPO response).
​

High reticulocyte count may indicate recent blood loss or effective iron therapy.
​

Erythrocyte Homeostasis (Feedback)

Drop in RBC count → hypoxemia in kidneys → increased EPO → stimulated bone marrow → RBC count rises in 3–4 days (negative feedback).
​

Stimuli for erythropoiesis: low atmospheric O₂, increased exercise, and hemorrhage.
​

RBC Life Cycle and Removal

RBC lifespan is about 120 days; they wear out from bending through capillaries and cannot repair due to lack of organelles.
​

Old RBCs are removed by fixed macrophages in spleen and liver; breakdown products are recycled.
​

Nutritional Requirements for RBC Production

Iron is a key requirement; daily losses through urine, feces, and bleeding are ~0.9 mg in men and 1.7 mg in women, requiring 5–20 mg/day intake.
​

Dietary iron: ferric (Fe³⁺) and ferrous (Fe²⁺); stomach acid converts Fe³⁺ to absorbable Fe²⁺.
​

Gastroferritin from stomach binds Fe²⁺ and transports it to intestine; iron then binds transferrin in blood and goes to bone marrow (for Hb), muscle (for myoglobin), and all cells (for cytochromes).
​

Liver stores excess iron as ferritin (Fe bound to apoferritin).
​

B₁₂ and folic acid are needed for rapid cell division; vitamin C and copper are cofactors for enzymes that synthesize RBCs.
​

Hemoglobin Structure and Transport Roles

Hemoglobin has four globin chains (2 alpha, 2 beta); each chain has a heme group binding one O₂ to Fe²⁺, so each Hb can carry four O₂.
​

Fetal hemoglobin uses gamma instead of beta chains.
​

Hemoglobin carries about 23% of CO₂ (bound to globin) and can transport nitric oxide/super‑nitric oxide, helping regulate blood pressure via vasodilation in lungs and tissues.
​

Hemoglobin and Iron Recycling

In macrophages, globin is broken down into amino acids; heme splits into Fe³⁺ and biliverdin.
​

Iron binds transferrin in blood, is stored as ferritin/hemosiderin in liver, muscle, and spleen, or used in bone marrow.
​

Biliverdin is converted to bilirubin; liver secretes bilirubin into bile, which intestinal bacteria convert to urobilinogen and stercobilin (brown pigment of feces). Some reabsorbed urobilinogen becomes urobilin, excreted in urine.
​

RBC Indices and Sex Differences

Hematocrit: men 42–52%; women 37–48%.
​

Hemoglobin concentration: men 13–18 g/dL; women 12–16 g/dL.
​

RBC count: men 4.6–6.2 million/µL; women 4.2–5.4 million/µL; values are lower in women due to less androgen stimulation and menstrual losses.
​

Polycythemia – Excess RBCs

Primary polycythemia: cancer of erythropoietic cell line; RBC count up to 11 million/µL, hematocrit ~80%.
​

Secondary polycythemia: from dehydration, emphysema, high altitude, or conditioning; RBC count up to ~8 million/µL.
​

Dangers: increased blood volume, pressure, and viscosity leading to embolism, stroke, or heart failure.
​

Anemia – Causes and Effects

Anemia: deficiency of RBCs or hemoglobin.
​

Causes:

Inadequate erythropoiesis or Hb synthesis (e.g., B₁₂ deficiency or lack of intrinsic factor → pernicious anemia, iron‑deficiency, kidney failure with low EPO, aplastic anemia from marrow failure).
​

Hemorrhagic anemia from blood loss.
​

Hemolytic anemia from RBC destruction or hereditary Hb defects like thalassemia.
​

Effects: tissue hypoxia and necrosis (shortness of breath, lethargy), low blood osmolarity causing tissue edema, and low viscosity causing tachycardia and low BP.
​

Sickle‑Cell Anemia (SCA)

SCA is a genetic defect in Hb (Hb‑S) where two amino acids are changed.
​

At low O₂, RBCs become sickle‑shaped, rupture easily, causing anemia and clot formation.
​

Common in populations from the “malaria belt” (Mediterranean, sub‑Saharan Africa, Asia); Hb‑S persists because heterozygotes have increased resistance to malaria as RBCs leak K⁺, killing the parasite.
​

Blood PDF – Module 3
(WBCs, Platelets, Hemostasis, Clotting, Anticoagulants, Blood Types)

Learn Items
WBC Types and Basic Features

Leukocytes (WBCs) have nuclei and no hemoglobin.
​

They are classified as granulocytes (neutrophils, eosinophils, basophils) or agranulocytes (monocytes, lymphocytes) based on presence of visible cytoplasmic granules.
​

Leukopoiesis and Lifespan

Committed progenitors (B and T progenitors, granulocyte‑macrophage CFUs) have receptors for colony‑stimulating factors released by mature WBCs in response to infection.
​

Red bone marrow stores and releases granulocytes and monocytes; some lymphocytes leave unfinished and complete development in thymus (T cells).
​

Granulocytes leave blood after ~8 hours and live about 5 more days; monocytes leave in ~20 hours and become macrophages that can live for years; some lymphocytes provide immunity for decades.
​

Neutrophils (Granulocytes)

Also called polymorphonuclear leukocytes (polys); nuclei have 2–5 lobes connected by thin strands, with older cells having more lobes.
​

Young neutrophils are “band cells” with horseshoe‑shaped nuclei.
​

They have fine, pale lilac granules, are 10–12 μm in diameter, and account for about 60–70% of circulating WBCs.
​

Platelets and Hemostasis Overview

Platelets are small cell fragments involved in clotting (thrombocytes).
​

Hemostasis includes vascular spasm, platelet plug formation, and blood clotting (coagulation).
​

Platelets release factors that help form plugs and support clot stabilization and vessel repair.
​

Clotting Cascade – General and Pathways

Prothrombinase can be generated by either the extrinsic or intrinsic pathway; it is the key trigger for the common pathway forming fibrin threads.
​

Extrinsic pathway: damaged tissues release tissue factor (thromboplastin, Factor III) activating Factor VII; in presence of Ca²⁺, Factor X combines with V to form prothrombinase—this pathway is rapid (seconds).
​

Intrinsic pathway: activation occurs when endothelium is damaged and platelets contact collagen (activating Factor XII) and when platelets release phospholipids; requires several minutes and involves Ca²⁺ and Factors XII, X, and V.
​

Final Common Pathway and Thrombin

In the presence of Ca²⁺, prothrombinase converts prothrombin into thrombin.
​

Thrombin converts soluble fibrinogen into insoluble fibrin threads and activates Factor XIII (fibrin‑stabilizing factor).
​

Thrombin has positive feedback effects: it accelerates formation of more prothrombinase and activates platelets to release phospholipids.
​

Enzyme amplification means each activated factor activates many molecules in the next step, producing rapid clotting.
​

Vitamin K and Clotting

Normal clotting requires adequate vitamin K, a fat‑soluble vitamin absorbed with dietary lipids; absorption is reduced if bile release is insufficient.
​

Vitamin K is needed by the liver to synthesize clotting Factors II (prothrombin), VII, IX, and X; gut bacteria in the large intestine also produce vitamin K.
​

Clot Retraction and Repair

Clot retraction occurs within about 30 minutes: trapped platelets release Factor XIII to stabilize fibrin; platelet pseudopods contract and pull fibrin threads, condensing the clot and drawing wound edges together.
​

Platelet‑derived growth factor from platelets and endothelial cells stimulates fibroblasts and smooth muscle cells to proliferate and repair damaged vessel wall.
​

Fibrinolysis – Clot Dissolution

Factor XII accelerates formation of kallikrein, which converts plasminogen to plasmin (a fibrin‑dissolving enzyme).
​

Plasmin breaks down fibrin; plasmin further promotes kallikrein formation, creating a positive feedback loop for clot dissolution.
​

The fibrinolytic system removes small, inappropriate clots and resolves clots at sites of completed repair.
​

Hemostatic Control and Natural Anticoagulants

Clotting remains localized because fibrin absorbs thrombin and rapid blood flow dilutes clotting factors; endothelial cells and WBCs produce prostacyclin, which opposes thromboxane A₂ (platelet adhesion and release).
​

Natural anticoagulants include antithrombin (from liver), which inactivates thrombin, and heparin (from basophils and mast cells), which interferes with formation of prothrombin activator.
​

Intravascular Clotting and Emboli

Thrombosis: clot (thrombus) forming in an unbroken vessel, often on rough endothelium or when blood flow is slow (stasis) allowing factor buildup.
​

The clot may dissolve or dislodge and travel as an embolus (clot, air bubble, or fat); pulmonary emboli lodge in lungs.
​

Low‑dose aspirin blocks thromboxane A₂ synthesis and reduces inappropriate clot formation, lowering risk of strokes, TIAs, and myocardial infarctions.
​

Anticoagulant and Thrombolytic Drugs

Anticoagulants:

Heparin: given during hemodialysis and surgery.
​

Warfarin (Coumadin): vitamin K antagonist that blocks synthesis of clotting factors; acts more slowly than heparin.
​

Stored banked blood is treated with citrate phosphate dextrose (CPD), which removes Ca²⁺ to prevent clotting.
​

Thrombolytic agents (e.g., streptokinase, tissue plasminogen activator/t‑PA) directly or indirectly activate plasminogen to dissolve clots.
​

Hemophilia

Genetic lack of one or more clotting factors; often sex‑linked recessive in males.
​

Hemophilia A: deficiency of Factor VIII (~83% of cases); Hemophilia B: deficiency of Factor IX (~15%); Hemophilia C: deficiency of Factor XI (autosomal, less severe because alternative activation exists).
​

Physical exertion can cause prolonged bleeding and severe pain; treatment includes plasma or purified factor transfusions, with Factor VIII now produced via transgenic bacteria.
​

Blood Types – ABO Antigens and Antibodies

RBC surface antigens (agglutinogens) A and B are inherited combinations of proteins, glycoproteins, and glycolipids; at least 26 blood group systems exist (ABO, Rh, Kell, Lewis, Kidd, Duffy, etc.).
​

Plasma antibodies (agglutinins) anti‑A and anti‑B are gamma globulins that recognize and bind foreign agglutinogens on RBCs.
​

These antibodies are responsible for RBC agglutination in mismatched transfusions.
​

Vessels PDF – Module 1
(Overview, Tunics, Arteries, Arterioles, Capillaries, Veins)

Learn Items
Major Vessel Types & Circulatory Layout

Three principal categories of vessels: arteries carry blood away from the heart, veins carry blood back to the heart, and capillaries connect the smallest arteries to the smallest veins.

The cardiovascular system is a closed system of tubes; venules collect blood from capillaries and merge to form veins, while arteries branch into arterioles and then capillaries.
​

Vasa vasorum are small blood vessels within the walls of large vessels that nourish their deeper tissues.

Vessel Wall Layers (Tunics)

Tunica interna (intima): innermost layer lining the lumen, made of simple squamous endothelium plus basement membrane and a thin layer of connective tissue; it acts as a selectively permeable barrier and smooth layer that repels blood cells and platelets.

Tunica media: middle and usually thickest layer, consisting of smooth muscle, collagen, and sometimes elastic tissue; responsible for vasoconstriction and vasodilation.

Tunica externa (adventitia): outermost layer of areolar connective tissue that anchors the vessel to adjacent tissues and provides passage for small nerves, lymphatic vessels, and the vasa vasorum.

Sympathetic Innervation of Vessels

Vascular smooth muscle is innervated by the sympathetic nervous system.
​

Increased sympathetic stimulation causes vasoconstriction (smooth muscle contraction), decreasing vessel diameter; injury to an artery or arteriole triggers vasospasm, reducing blood loss.
​

Decreased stimulation or certain chemicals (nitric oxide, K⁺, H⁺, lactic acid) promote vasodilation, increasing vessel diameter.
​

Arteries – Conducting (Elastic) Arteries

Conducting (elastic or large) arteries are the largest, including the aorta, pulmonary trunk, common carotid, subclavian, and common iliac arteries.

Their tunica media contains perforated sheets of elastic tissue alternating with thin layers of smooth muscle, collagen, and elastic fibers.
​

They expand during systole and recoil during diastole, helping to dampen blood pressure fluctuations.
​

Arteries – Distributing (Muscular) Arteries

Distributing (muscular or medium) arteries are smaller branches that distribute blood to specific organs, such as brachial, femoral, splenic, and renal arteries.

In these arteries, smooth muscle layers make up about three‑quarters of wall thickness, allowing strong vasoconstriction and vasodilation.
​

Arterioles and Metarterioles

Arterioles are small arteries delivering blood to capillaries; their tunica media has only a few layers of smooth muscle.
​

Metarterioles branch into capillary beds; precapillary sphincters regulate whether blood enters the capillaries or bypasses them via a thoroughfare channel.
​

Vasomotion is the intermittent contraction and relaxation of sphincters, allowing capillary beds to fill 5–10 times per minute.
​

Capillaries – Microcirculation and Structure

Capillaries are microscopic vessels connecting arterioles to venules; they are found near almost every cell but are most extensive in active tissues like muscles, liver, kidneys, and brain.
​

Their walls are a single layer of simple squamous endothelium and a basement membrane, making them thin enough for exchange.
​

Their primary function is exchange of nutrients and wastes between blood and tissue fluid; capillary beds are absent in epithelia, cornea, lens of eye, and cartilage.
​

Capillary Types

Continuous capillaries: have intercellular clefts (small gaps) between endothelial cells; found in skeletal muscle, smooth muscle, connective tissues, and lungs.
​

Fenestrated capillaries: have many pores (fenestrations) in the plasma membrane; found in kidneys, small intestine, choroid plexuses, ciliary processes, and endocrine glands.
​

Sinusoids: have very large fenestrations and incomplete basement membrane; found in liver, bone marrow, spleen, anterior pituitary, and parathyroid glands.
​

Veins and Venules – General Features

Venules: small veins that collect blood from capillaries; proximal venules are quite porous and exchange fluid with tissues like capillaries.
​

As venules enlarge, they resemble small veins, with sparse smooth muscle and fibroblasts; their porous endothelium allows WBCs to exit into tissues.
​

Veins have proportionally thinner walls than arteries of similar diameter, with less smooth muscle and no internal or external elastic lamina.
​

Veins have lower average pressure (~10 mmHg), expand easily, and act as high‑capacitance vessels; venous valves (folds of tunica interna) prevent backflow and aid skeletal muscle in upward blood flow.
​

Venous sinuses (e.g., coronary sinus, dural venous sinuses) have thin walls, large lumens, and no smooth muscle.
​

Varicose Veins

Varicose veins are twisted, dilated superficial veins caused by leaky venous valves (congenital or from prolonged standing or pregnancy).
​

Valve failure allows backflow and pooling, increasing pressure and forcing fluid into tissues, leading to inflamed, tender surrounding tissue.
​

Deep veins are less susceptible due to the support of surrounding muscles.
​

​Vessels PDF – Module 2
(Hemodynamics, Capillary Exchange, BP, Resistance, Venous Return, Edema)

Learn Items
Capillary Exchange Mechanisms

Exchange occurs only across capillary walls between blood and interstitial fluid via three routes: intercellular clefts, fenestrations, or through endothelial cytoplasm.
​

Diffusion is the main mechanism (down concentration gradients); lipid‑soluble substances (steroid hormones, O₂, CO₂) diffuse through lipid bilayer, while water‑soluble substances (glucose, electrolytes) pass through channels, fenestrations, or clefts.
​

Large proteins are held back by the endothelium.
​

Transcytosis (endocytosis/exocytosis in vesicles) moves large lipid‑insoluble molecules like insulin or maternal antibodies across the endothelium.
​

Bulk Flow – Filtration and Reabsorption

Bulk flow moves large amounts of dissolved or suspended material in response to pressure from high to low pressure areas.
​

Filtration: movement out into interstitial fluid, promoted by blood hydrostatic pressure and interstitial osmotic pressure.
​

Reabsorption: movement back into capillaries, promoted by blood colloid osmotic pressure (COP, mainly from albumin).
​

Net filtration pressure = balance of these forces; Starling’s law states that reabsorbed volume is almost equal to filtered volume (~85% reabsorbed, excess collected by lymphatics).
​

Net Filtration Pressure Dynamics

Arterial end of capillary: net outward pressure ~10 mmHg (higher hydrostatic pressure).
​

Venous end: net inward pressure ~9 mmHg (higher COP relative to hydrostatic pressure).
​

About 85% of filtered fluid is reabsorbed; remaining ~3 L/day is returned by lymphatics.
​

Edema – Causes

Edema is abnormal increase in interstitial fluid when filtration exceeds reabsorption.
​

Excess filtration: increased BP (hypertension) or increased capillary permeability (e.g., histamine release).
​

Inadequate reabsorption: decreased plasma proteins (low COP) from liver disease, burns, malnutrition, or kidney disease.
​

Not noticeable until ~30% above normal.
​

Edema Consequences and Triggers

Poor venous return: congestive heart failure → pulmonary edema; insufficient muscle activity; kidney failure → water retention and hypertension.
​

Obstructed lymphatic drainage → edema.
​

Consequences: circulatory shock (low blood volume/BP), tissue necrosis (poor O₂/waste removal), pulmonary edema (suffocation), cerebral edema (headaches, nausea, seizures, coma).
​

Hemodynamics – Key Factors

Hemodynamics involves pressure differences driving flow, velocity of flow, volume of flow, blood pressure, resistance, and venous return.
​

Blood flow velocity is inversely proportional to total cross‑sectional area (slowest in capillaries for exchange, fastest in aorta).
​

Circulation time: time for a blood drop to go from right atrium back to right atrium.
​

Blood Pressure and Volume Flow

BP is highest in aorta (~120 mmHg systolic, 80 diastolic); falls steadily in systemic circulation (35 mmHg entering capillaries, 0 mmHg at right atrium).
​

Cardiac output = SV × HR; BP rises with increased HR/CO or blood volume.
​

Arterial elasticity (expansion/recoil) maintains steady flow, smooths pressure fluctuations, and reduces stress on small arteries; less elastic arteries with age raise BP.
​

Resistance to Flow

Resistance comes from friction between blood and vessel walls; factors include vessel radius, blood viscosity, and vessel length.
​

Blood flow is proportional to the fourth power of vessel radius (r⁴); halving radius reduces flow to 1/16th (arterioles control BP by changing diameter).
​

Increased viscosity (e.g., dehydration, polycythemia) increases resistance; longer vessels increase resistance (obesity worsens this).
​

Systemic vascular resistance is the total of these factors.
​

Blood Flow Velocity and Laminar Flow

Laminar flow: blood flows in layers with faster flow in center; small vessel radius lowers average velocity, large radius increases it.
​

Velocity decreases from aorta to capillaries (greater distance, smaller radii, larger total cross‑sectional area) and increases from capillaries to vena cava as vessels merge.
​

Capillary flow is slowest (~0.1 cm/sec) to allow exchange.
​

Mechanisms of Venous Return

Pressure gradient: venous pressure ~7–13 mmHg toward the heart (venules ~12–18 mmHg to central venous ~5 mmHg).
​

Skeletal muscle pump: muscle contraction squeezes veins, pushing blood toward heart (valves prevent backflow).
​

Thoracic pump: inhalation lowers thoracic pressure and raises abdominal pressure, forcing blood upward; central venous pressure fluctuates (2 mmHg inhale, 6 mmHg exhale).
​

Cardiac suction: expanding atrial space pulls blood in.
​

Exercise and Venous Return

Exercise increases venous return via faster/stronger heart (↑ CO/BP), vasodilation in skeletal muscle/lungs/heart, increased respiratory rate (thoracic pump), and skeletal muscle pump.
​

Inactivity causes venous pooling (low venous pressure insufficient for upward flow), leading to low CO, dizziness, or syncope; prevented by leg muscle tensing.
​

Shock and Homeostasis

Shock: cardiovascular failure to deliver enough O₂/nutrients, causing inadequate perfusion and switch to anaerobic respiration → lactic acid buildup → cell/tissue damage and death.
​

Blood Pressure & Lymphatic PDF – Module 1
(Blood Pressure Basics, Pulse Points, BP Measurement, Lymphatic Overview & Organs)

Learn Items
Cardiac Cycle and Blood Pressure

The cardiac cycle is one contraction (systole) and relaxation (diastole) of the heart, lasting about 0.8 seconds.
​

The dicrotic notch is a small secondary pressure increase at the beginning of diastole, caused by closure of aortic/pulmonary valves.
​

Pulse pressure is the difference between systolic and diastolic pressures (~40 mmHg).
​

Heart Sounds in the Cardiac Cycle

First and second heart sounds (S₁ and S₂) are often described as “lubb‑dupp” and are due to closing of the valves.
​

S₁ (“lubb”): closure of AV valves at start of systole.
​

S₂ (“dupp”): closure of semilunar valves at start of diastole.
​

Pulse Points

Common sites for taking pulse: carotid, radial, brachial, dorsalis pedis (dorsal foot artery), posterior tibial.
​

Taking a Blood Pressure – Step‑by‑Step

Place cuff on bare upper arm 1 inch above elbow bend, tight enough for two fingertips under top edge.
​

Position stethoscope disk under cuff on inner side of upper arm.
​

Place earpieces facing forward (toward nose tip), rest gauge in palm of cuffed arm.
​

Inflate cuff rapidly to 30 points above usual systolic pressure, then slowly deflate while listening.
​

Lymphatic System – Three Functions

Fluid recovery: reabsorbs excess interstitial fluid (~15% of filtered fluid not returned by capillaries) and returns it to blood.
​

Immunity: tissue fluid (lymph) is filtered through lymph nodes containing immune cells before returning to bloodstream.
​

Lipid absorption: lacteals in small intestine villi absorb dietary lipids.
​

Lymphatic Organs – Thymus

Thymus: bilobed organ between sternum and aortic arch; microscopic features include cortex, medulla, and Hassall’s corpuscles.
​

Lymphatic Organs – Spleen

Spleen: in left hypochondriac region, inferior to diaphragm and posterolateral to stomach; has white pulp and red pulp.
​

Lymphatic Organs – Lymph Nodes

Lymph nodes: most numerous (~450 in adults), located in cervical, axillary, intestinal, and inguinal regions.
​

Microscopic: capsule, cortex with lymphoid follicles, medulla.
​

Lymphatic Vessels and Flow

Lymph flows through lymphatic vessels (lymphatics); openings are gaps between endothelial cells, anchored by filaments.
​

Right lymphatic duct: formed by convergence of right jugular, subclavian, and bronchomediastinal trunks.
​

Thoracic duct: drains from cisterna chyli (sac) and empties into left subclavian vein.
​

Other Lymphatic Structures

Appendix: contains abundant lymphoid nodules (follicles).
​

Tonsils: three sets – pharyngeal (adenoids), palatine (pair), lingual (numerous); have crypts and lymphoid follicles.
​

​Lymphatic & Immune PDF – Module 1
(Lymphatic Functions, Vessels/Flow, Cells, Tissues, Organs)

Learn Items
Lymphatic and Immune Systems Overview

The lymphatic and immune systems protect the body from infection and disease.
​

Lymphatic system consists of organs, vessels, and lymph fluid (similar to interstitial fluid).
​

Key organs: red bone marrow, thymus, spleen, lymph nodes, diffuse lymphatic tissue (tonsils, adenoids, Peyer’s patches).
​

Functions of the Lymphatic System

Immunity: filters fluids from capillary beds through lymph nodes where immune cells respond to foreign cells/chemicals.
​

Lipid absorption: lacteals in small intestine absorb dietary lipids.
​

Fluid recovery: absorbs plasma proteins and fluid (2–4 L/day) from tissues and returns it to bloodstream; interference causes severe edema.
​

Lymph and Lymphatic Capillaries

Lymph: clear, colorless fluid similar to plasma but with much less protein.
​

Lymphatic capillaries: closed at one end, tethered by protein filaments; endothelial cells loosely overlap to form valve‑like flaps (open with high interstitial pressure, close with low pressure), allowing bacteria/cells to enter but not exit.
​

Found throughout body except avascular tissues (cartilage, epidermis, cornea); in GI tract called lacteals (contain chyle).
​

Lymphatic Vessels

Larger vessels have three layers: tunica interna (endothelium + valves), tunica media (elastic fibers + smooth muscle), tunica externa (thin outer layer).
​

Route of Lymph Flow

Lymphatic capillaries → collecting vessels (pass through lymph nodes) → lymphatic trunks → collecting ducts.
​

Right lymphatic duct: drains right arm, right side of head/thorax, empties into right subclavian vein.
​

Thoracic duct: larger/longer, begins as cisterna chyli (abdominal sac), drains below diaphragm + left arm/head/neck/thorax, empties into left subclavian vein.
​

Mechanisms of Lymph Flow

Low pressure/speed; moved by rhythmic contractions of lymphatic vessels (stretching stimulates contraction), skeletal muscle pump, thoracic pump (abdominal to thoracic flow), valves preventing backflow, and rapid bloodstream suction in subclavian veins.
​

Exercise significantly increases lymphatic return.
​

Lymphatic Cells

T lymphocytes: mature in thymus.
​

B lymphocytes: activation leads to plasma cells producing antibodies.
​

Antigen‑presenting cells (APCs): macrophages (from monocytes), dendritic cells (epidermis/mucous membranes/lymph organs), reticular cells (stroma of lymph organs).
​

Lymphatic Tissue

Diffuse lymphatic tissue: lymphocytes in mucous membranes/CT of organs; mucosa‑associated lymphatic tissue (MALT) prevalent in exterior passages.
​

Lymphatic nodules: dense oval lymphocyte masses that congregate in response to pathogens; Peyer patches are more permanent clusters at small/large intestine junction.
​

Lymphatic Organs Overview

Encapsulated with CT capsules at defined sites: lymph nodes, tonsils, thymus, spleen.
​

Lymph nodes: in cervical/axillary/inguinal (surface) and thoracic/abdominal/pelvic (deep); scattered near mammary glands, axillae, groin.
​

Tonsils: guard pharynx entrance.
​

Thymus: between sternum and aortic arch.
​

Spleen: inferior to diaphragm, dorsolateral to stomach.
​

Lymph Nodes Structure and Function

Bean‑shaped, up to 1 inch long, along lymphatic vessels.
​

Stroma: capsule, trabeculae, reticular fibers.
​

Parenchyma: cortex (lymphatic nodules with germinal centers containing dendritic cells, APCs, macrophages; B cells → plasma cells) and medulla (B cells/plasma cells in medullary cords).
​

One‑way flow: afferent vessels in, sinuses to efferent vessels out at hilus; only nodes filter lymph.
​

Cancer Metastasis via Lymphatics

Malignant tumors spread via lymph/blood; secondary sites predictable by lymph flow direction from primary site.
​

Cancerous nodes: firm, enlarged, nontender; infected nodes: tender, not firm.
​

​

Lymphatic & Immune PDF – Module 2
(Lymph Nodes, Organs, Immunology Basics, Nonspecific Resistance)

Learn Items
Lymph Nodes – Flow and Structure

Flow is one‑way: afferent vessels → sinuses → efferent vessels exiting at hilus; only lymph nodes filter lymph.
​

Cortex: lymphatic nodules with germinal centers (dendritic cells, APCs, macrophages); B cells proliferate into antibody‑secreting plasma cells.
​

Medulla: B cells and plasma cells in medullary cords.
​

Cancer Metastasis and Lymph Nodes

Characteristic of malignant tumors; cancer cells travel via lymph or blood to establish new tumors at secondary sites, predictable by lymph flow direction from primary site.
​

Cancerous nodes: firm, enlarged, nontender; infected nodes: tender, not firm.
​

Tonsils Location and Structure

Palatine tonsils: pair at posterior margin of oral cavity (most often infected).
​

Lingual tonsils: pair at root of tongue.
​

Pharyngeal tonsil (adenoid): single on pharyngeal wall.
​

Tonsils covered by epithelium; pathogens enter crypts and meet lymphocytes.
​

Thymus Gland Structure

Large in infants (~70 g), atrophied in adults (~3 g); bilobed in mediastinum with capsule/trabeculae dividing into lobules.
​

Cortex: tightly packed lymphocytes/macrophages.
​

Medulla: reticular epithelial cells produce thymic hormones; contains Hassall’s corpuscles.
​

Spleen Structure and Functions

Parenchyma: red pulp (erythrocyte‑filled sinuses), white pulp (lymphocytes/macrophages around splenic artery branches).
​

Functions: fetal blood production, blood reservoir, RBC disposal, immune reactions (filters blood, detects antigens).
​

Immunology Overview

Resistance wards off disease; susceptibility is lack of resistance.
​

Nonspecific resistance: general mechanisms against wide range of pathogens (no specific response).
​

Specific resistance/immunity: fights specific pathogens via cell‑mediated (T cells) or antibody‑mediated (B cells).
​

Nonspecific Resistance – Skin & Mucous Membranes

Mechanical: keratinized epidermis (shedding removes microbes), mucous (traps microbes), cilia/mucus (move to throat), washing (tears, urine, saliva).
​

Chemical: sebum (inhibits bacteria/fungi), perspiration lysozymes (break down bacteria), acidic pH (gastric juice, vaginal secretions destroys bacteria).
​

Leukocytes in Cutaneous Defenses

Neutrophils: phagocytize bacteria, create killing zone via degranulation (lysosomes discharge) and respiratory burst (O₂⁻, H₂O₂, HClO).
​

Eosinophils: phagocytize antigen‑antibody complexes/allergens/inflammatory chemicals; antiparasitic effects via enzyme release.
​

Internal Nonspecific Defenses – Antimicrobial Proteins

Interferons: produced by virus‑infected lymphocytes/macrophages; diffuse to neighbors inducing antiviral proteins; activate NK cells/macrophages; destroy infected/cancer cells.
​

Complement: inactive plasma proteins activated by pathogens to enhance inflammation/phagocytosis.
​

Transferrins: iron‑binding proteins that inhibit bacterial growth by limiting available iron.
​

Natural Killer (NK) Cells & Phagocytes

NK cells: kill microbes/tumor cells displaying abnormal MHC; found in blood/spleen/lymph nodes/marrow.
​

Phagocytes: neutrophils/macrophages ingest microbes/particles; fixed macrophages in tissues (histiocytes/skin, Kupffer cells/liver, alveolar macrophages/lungs, microglia/brain, etc.); wandering macrophages in most tissues.
​

Phagocytosis Steps

Chemotaxis: attraction to chemicals from damaged tissues/complement/microbial products.
​

Adherence: attachment to phagocyte membrane.
​

Ingestion: engulf by pseudopods → phagosome.
​

Digestion/killing: merge with lysosome (enzymes), lethal oxidants; exocytosis of residual body.
​

Inflammation – Signs and Mobilization

Defensive response to injury limiting pathogen spread, destroying them, removing debris, repairing tissue; -itis suffix indicates inflammation.
​

Cardinal signs: redness (hyperemia), swelling (edema from ↑permeability), heat (hyperemia), pain (bradykinin/prostaglandins, nerve pressure).
​

Damaged cells/basophils/mast cells secrete bradykinin/histamine/leukotrienes → vasodilation (hyperemia: redness/heat, ↑metabolism/healing), ↑capillary permeability (allows WBCs/antibodies/complement/fibrinogen).
​

Fibrinogen clots to trap bacteria/scaffold repair; heparin prevents clotting in injury site.
​

Inflammation – Leukocyte Deployment

Margination: leukocytes adhere to vessel walls via cell adhesion molecules.
​

Diapedesis: leukocytes squeeze between endothelial cells into tissues.
​

Chemotaxis attracts leukocytes (neutrophils first); phagocytosis + respiratory burst + cytokines recruit macrophages/T cells.
​

Inflammation – Cleanup and Repair

Monocytes → macrophages for cleanup (arrive 8–12 hours).
​

Edema ↓venous flow but ↑lymphatic removal of bacteria/debris.
​

Pus: tissue fluid, debris, dying neutrophils, microbes.
​

PDGF from platelets/endothelium stimulates fibroblasts/collagen for repair; hyperemia provides materials/heat.
​

Pain limits part use for healing.
​

Abscesses and Ulcers

Abscess: pus accumulation in confined space (pimples/boils).
​

Ulcer: open sore; common in legs of diabetics with poor circulation (stasis ulcers from poor O₂/nutrients).
​

d) All phagocytosis
Answer: b

​Lymphatic & Immune PDF – Module 3
(NK Cells, Antimicrobial Proteins, Fever, Cytokines, T/B Cells, Cellular Immunity)

Learn Items
Natural Killer (NK) Cells

Derived from T lymphocyte precursors; specialized for “self from funky self” (abnormal MHC antigens).
​

Kill variety of microbes and tumor cells; found in blood, spleen, lymph nodes, red marrow.
​

Attack cells displaying abnormal MHC antigens.
​

NK Cell Action – Perforin

NK cells secrete perforin (punches holes in target cell membrane) and other toxic substances.
​

Antimicrobial Proteins

Interferons: polypeptides from virus‑infected lymphocytes/macrophages; diffuse to neighbors inducing antiviral proteins; activate NK cells/macrophages; destroy infected host cells; anticancer effects.
​

Complement: inactive plasma proteins activated by pathogens via classical or alternate pathways; mechanisms: inflammation, opsonization (phagocytosis promotion), cytolysis (membrane attack complex).
​

Transferrins: iron‑binding proteins inhibiting bacterial growth by reducing available iron.
​

Complement Pathways and Actions

Classical pathway: begins with C1 activation.
​

Alternate pathway: begins with C3 activation.
​

Both lead to inflammation, enhanced phagocytosis, or microbe bursting; membrane attack complex (C5b–C9 ring) causes cytolysis.
​

Fever

Defense mechanism promoting interferon, metabolic rate/tissue repair, inhibiting pathogen reproduction.
​

Macrophage cytokine interleukin‑1 (pyrogen) stimulates hypothalamus to secrete PGE, resetting thermostat higher.
​

Stages: onset, stadium, defervescence; >105°F may cause delirium, 111–115°F coma/death.
​

Cytokines and Cytokine Therapy

Small protein hormones from lymphocytes/APCs involved in immune responses.
​

Alpha‑interferon: treats Kaposi’s sarcoma, genital herpes, hepatitis B/C, leukemias.
​

Beta‑interferon: treats multiple sclerosis.
​

Interleukin‑2: treats cancer (with side effects).
​

Lymphocytes in Specific Immunity

Specific immunity depends on lymphocytes: ~80% T cells (cell‑mediated), 15% B cells (antibody‑mediated), 5% NK cells (nonspecific).
​

T Lymphocytes (T Cells)

Fetal stem cells colonize thymus for 2–3 days; thymosins stimulate antigen receptor production → immunocompetent T cells.
​

T Cell Selection in Thymus

Negative selection: T cells unable to bind reticular epithelium or reacting to self antigens undergo clonal deletion (death), anergy (inactive), achieving self‑tolerance (~1 in 100 survive).
​

Positive selection: T cells binding MHC on epithelium (not self‑reactive) divide into clones and leave to colonize lymphatic tissues.
​

Cellular (Cell‑Mediated) Immunity

T lymphocytes attack foreign cells/diseased host cells via four T cell classes: cytotoxic (killer) T cells (attack), helper T cells (promote T/B/nonspecific), suppressor T cells (limit attack), memory T cells (future immunity).
​

Cytotoxic T Cell Activation

CD8 cell receptor binds foreign antigen fragment on MHC‑I; costimulation from helper T cell cytokine prevents accidental response.
​

Leads to clonal expansion into cytotoxic T cells and memory Tc cells in secondary organs like lymph nodes.
​

Cytotoxic T Cells (Tc/CD8)

Recognize antigen fragments on MHC‑I (virus‑infected, tumor cells, transplants).
​

Activation requires MHC‑I binding + helper T cytokine costimulation → clonal selection.
​

Migrate to infection/tumor; attack by perforin (membrane holes), lymphotoxin (DNA fragmentation enzymes), gamma‑interferon (activates phagocytes).
​

Tumor necrosis factor kills cancer cells in 2–3 days.
​

Immunological Surveillance

Immune system detects tumor antigens on cancerous cells (especially virus‑induced); cytotoxic T cells, macrophages, NK cells destroy them.
​

Immunosuppressive drugs (e.g., transplant patients) increase viral cancer risk.
​

Graft Rejection

Transplant triggers cell‑ and antibody‑mediated responses; histocompatibility antigen match reduces rejection.
​

Cyclosporine inhibits IL‑2 secretion by helper T cells (little B cell effect, preserves some resistance).
​

​Respiratory PDF – Module 1
(Upper/Lower Respiratory Tract, Alveoli, Lungs, Pleura)

Learn Items
Respiratory System Overview

The respiratory system provides large aerial surface for gas exchange between air and blood, moves air to/from lungs, maintains blood pH, produces sounds, eliminates water‑soluble wastes from blood, contains receptors for smell/taste/reflexes, traps/reflects particles.

Upper Respiratory Tract

Nose/nasal cavity/pharynx (shared with digestive).

Nose: external nose (root, bridge, dorsum nasi, philtrum, apex, nostrils/nares), nasal cavity (vestibule, olfactory area, respiratory area/respiratory mucosa).

Nasal conchae (superior/middle/inferior): project medially from lateral walls; divide cavity into meatuses.

Functions: warms/humidifies air, detects odors, filters/lights dust/pollen/microbes.

Nasal Cavity Details

Nasal septum: perpendicular plate of ethmoid + vomer; lateral walls: perpendicular plate of palatine, medial pterygoid plate of sphenoid, inferior/middle/superior nasal conchae.

Paranasal sinuses: frontal, sphenoidal, maxillary, ethmoidal; drain into nasal cavity/meatuses.

Nasolacrimal duct drains tears into inferior meatus.

Pharynx

Muscular tube ~5 inches long from internal nares to larynx/esophagus entrance.

Nasopharynx (behind nose, superior to soft palate): pharyngeal tonsil (adenoid), pharyngotympanic (auditory) tubes open here.

Oropharynx (posterior oral cavity): palatine tonsils, lingual tonsils at tongue base.

Laryngopharynx (inferior, posterior larynx): opens into esophagus/larynx.

Lower Respiratory Tract

Larynx, trachea, bronchi, bronchioles, alveoli.

Larynx

Short passageway connecting laryngopharynx/trachea (~2 inches, C3–C6); prevents food/air aspiration, voice production, pressure regulation in thoracic cavity.

Cartilages: thyroid (Adam’s apple), cricoid, epiglottis (elastic cartilage, lid over glottis), arytenoid/corniculate/cuneiform.

Vocal folds: vestibular folds (false vocal cords), vocal folds (true vocal cords, glottis between).

Trachea

~4–5 inches long, ~1 inch diameter; C‑shaped hyaline cartilage rings (16–20), posterior open to esophagus (trachealis muscle).

Mucosa: pseudostratified ciliated columnar epithelium + goblet cells + lamina propria + submucosa (seromucous glands).

Bifurcates at carina (T4–T5) into main (primary) bronchi.

Bronchi and Bronchial Tree

Right main bronchus: shorter/wider/more vertical; left main bronchus: longer/narrower.

Lobar (secondary) bronchi (right: 3, left: 2); segmental (tertiary) bronchi (~10 right, 8–10 left); ~25 generations of bronchioles.

Bronchi have progressively less cartilage/more smooth muscle; respiratory bronchioles have some alveoli; alveolar ducts/sacs/terminal alveoli.

Alveoli and Gas Exchange

~300–400 million alveoli (~150–200 m² surface area); simple squamous epithelium (type I pneumocytes for diffusion, type II cuboidal secrete surfactant).

Alveolar macrophages (dust cells), elastic fibers.

Respiratory membrane: fused basement membranes + interstitial fluid.

Lungs and Pleura

Lungs occupy most thoracic cavity (apex above first rib, base on diaphragm); right: 3 lobes (superior/middle/inferior), left: 2 lobes (superior/inferior) + lingula.

Fissures: oblique (both lungs), horizontal (right lung only).

Root: main bronchus, pulmonary artery/veins, nerves, lymphatics; covered by visceral pleura.

Pleura: visceral (lungs), parietal (thoracic wall/mediastinum/diaphragm); pleural cavity with serous fluid (~50 mL).

Endocrine PDF – Module 1
(Endocrine Glands, Hormones, Hypothalamus-Pituitary, Thyroid, Parathyroid)

Learn Items (from file:14)
Endocrine System Overview

Endocrine glands secrete hormones into bloodstream (no ducts).
​

Regulates metabolism, growth, reproduction, stress response via chemical messengers.
​

Target cells have specific receptors; effects slower but longer-lasting than nervous system.
​

Hormone Actions

Hormones bind receptors, alter gene expression or enzyme activity.
​

Water-soluble: use second messengers (cAMP).
​

Lipid-soluble: enter cells, affect transcription.
​

Hypothalamus & Pituitary

Hypothalamus: master control, produces releasing/inhibiting hormones.
​

Anterior pituitary: tropic hormones (TSH, ACTH, FSH/LH, GH, prolactin).
​

Posterior pituitary: stores/releases ADH, oxytocin from hypothalamus.
​

Thyroid Gland

Follicles produce T3/T4 (thyroxine — increase metabolism).
​

Parafollicular cells produce calcitonin (lowers blood Ca²⁺).
​

Regulated by TSH from anterior pituitary.
​

Parathyroid Glands

On posterior thyroid surface; secrete PTH (raises blood Ca²⁺).
​

Actions: osteoclast activation, renal Ca reabsorption, vitamin D activation.
​

Antagonizes calcitonin.
​

Adrenal Glands

Cortex: mineralocorticoids (aldosterone — Na⁺ retention), glucocorticoids (cortisol — stress, glucose), androgens.
​

Medulla: epinephrine/norepinephrine (fight-or-flight).
​

c) Increases metabolism

Endocrine PDF – Module 2
(Adrenal Glands, Pancreas, Gonads, Other Organs, Feedback)

Learn Items
Adrenal Glands

Adrenal cortex (outer): zona glomerulosa (mineralocorticoids like aldosterone — Na⁺ retention, K⁺ excretion), zona fasciculata (glucocorticoids like cortisol — glucose production, anti-inflammatory), zona reticularis (androgens).

Adrenal medulla (inner): chromaffin cells secrete epinephrine/norepinephrine (sympathetic response: ↑HR, ↑BP, glycogenolysis).
​

Regulated by ACTH (cortex), sympathetic NS (medulla).
​

Pancreas

Islets of Langerhans: α-cells (glucagon — ↑blood glucose via glycogenolysis), β-cells (insulin — ↓blood glucose via uptake/storage), δ-cells (somatostatin — inhibits both).
​

Regulated by blood glucose levels (high → insulin; low → glucagon).
​

Gonads

Ovaries: granulosa/theca cells produce estrogen/progesterone (follicular phase estrogen, luteal phase progesterone).

Testes: interstitial (Leydig) cells produce testosterone (spermatogenesis, secondary sex characteristics).
​

Regulated by FSH/LH from anterior pituitary.
​

Other Endocrine Organs

Pineal: melatonin (circadian rhythm, puberty inhibition).
​

Thymus: thymosin/thymopoietin (T-cell maturation).
​

Heart: ANP (↓BP via natriuresis).
​

Kidneys: erythropoietin (RBC production), renin (BP regulation).
​

GI tract: gastrin, secretin, CCK (digestion).
​

Hormone Regulation

Negative feedback: most common (e.g., high cortisol inhibits CRH/ACTH).
​

Positive feedback: rare (e.g., oxytocin in labor).
​

Circadian rhythms (e.g., cortisol peaks morning).
​

Disorders

Hypersecretion: Cushing's (↑cortisol — moon face, buffalo hump), Graves' (↑thyroid — weight loss).
​

Hyposecretion: Addison's (↓cortisol — fatigue, low BP), diabetes mellitus (↓insulin).
​

Systems Covered
1. Heart (files 4,5,10,12)
​
Module 1: Anatomy (chambers, valves, coronary circulation)

Module 2: Conduction (SA/AV nodes, ECG waves)

Module 3: Cardiac cycle (systole/diastole, output CO=HR×SV)

Key Quiz Items: Chordae tendineae prevent valve prolapse; ECG P-QRS-T; Frank-Starling law.

2. Blood (files 2,18,14 partial)
​
Module 1: Plasma (albumins/globulins/fibrinogen), RBCs (Hb transport, erythropoiesis)

Module 2: WBCs (neutrophils 60-70%, eosinophils parasites), platelets

Module 3: Hemostasis (vascular spasm, platelet plug, coagulation cascade)

Key Quiz Items: Hematocrit men 42-52%; sickle-cell HbS; extrinsic pathway (tissue factor).

3. Vessels (files 1,7,9,15,16)
​
Module 1: Structure (tunica intima/media/externa; elastic vs muscular arteries)

Module 2: Capillaries (continuous/fenestrated/sinusoids), exchange (diffusion, Starling forces)

Module 3: Hemodynamics (BP=CO×PR; Poiseuille F∝r⁴; venous return pumps)

Key Quiz Items: Vasa vasorum in large vessels; edema from ↑filtration; MAP=(SBP+2DBP)/3.

4. Blood Pressure/Lymphatic (files 3,17)
​
Module 1: BP regulation (baroreceptors, chemoreceptors, RAAS)

Module 2: Lymph flow (capillaries → trunks → ducts), edema causes

Key Quiz Items: Hypertension >140/90; thoracic pump aids venous return.

5. Lymphatic/Immune (files 8,13)
​
Module 1: Lymph nodes, spleen, thymus, tonsils

Module 2: Nonspecific (NK cells, interferons, complement, fever)

Module 3: Specific (T cells: cytotoxic/helper; B cells/plasma; cytokines)

Key Quiz Items: Classical complement starts C1; negative T-cell selection (self-tolerance); perforin from NK/Tc.

6. Endocrine (files 6,11,14)
​
Module 1: Hypothalamus-pituitary axis, thyroid (T3/T4), parathyroid (PTH vs calcitonin)

Module 2: Adrenal (cortex: aldosterone/cortisol; medulla: epi/NE), pancreas (insulin/glucagon), gonads, others (ANP, melatonin)

Key Quiz Items: Negative feedback (cortisol ↓CRH/ACTH); glucagon α-cells; Cushing's ↑cortisol.
